title: Ekalavya and Drona
body: A story in the Adi Parvan of the Mahabharata tells of Drona, a Brahmana who taught archery to the Kuru princes. Ekalavya, a forest-dwelling nishada, asked to become his pupil, but Drona, 'who knew the dharma', refused. Ekalavya went back to the forest, made a clay image of Drona, treated it as his teacher and practised until he became a superb archer. When the princes discovered his skill, Arjuna reminded Drona of his promise that no pupil would be his equal. Drona went to Ekalavya, who honoured him as his teacher. Drona demanded his right thumb as his fee, and Ekalavya cut it off at once. After that he could no longer shoot as fast as before, and no one was better than Arjuna.

title: Excavations at Hastinapura
body: In 1951-52 the archaeologist B.B. Lal excavated at a village named Hastinapura in Meerut (Uttar Pradesh), in the Upper Ganga doab where the Kuru kingdom was located. He found five occupational levels. For the second phase (c. twelfth-seventh centuries BCE) he found no definite house plans, but walls of mud and mud-bricks, and mud-plaster with reed-marks suggesting reed walls plastered with mud. For the third phase (c. sixth-third centuries BCE) houses were built of mud-brick and burnt bricks, with soakage jars, brick drains and terracotta ring-wells. The Adi Parvan, by contrast, describes Hastinapura as a city 'bursting like the ocean, packed with hundreds of mansions', with gateways, arches and turrets like massing clouds.
